Three aircraft.
One calculation engine.

Bf 109 F-4 • P-47B • P-51B-15. Shared physics · documented DB 601E gear correction · honest cross-aircraft speed/climb checks · RAF Mosquito and Focke-Wulf stores trials.

Experimental research prototype — NOT validated sustained-turn data. All speed, load-factor and turn curves depend on assumed Oswald efficiency, installed propeller performance and clean-wing maximum lift. The 109 and P-47 historical engines do not have equal source confidence.

v1.8 / Real historical holdouts, IL-2 & DCS comparisons, and a physics-based propeller experiment

Decision: preserve C as the working model. The new profile D is a transparent actuator-disk momentum-energy calculation based on NACA's induced-loss treatment with one universal, assumed 85% profile/installation power fraction. D has the physically expected negative η versus low-speed blade-power-loading slope; C is slightly positive. D helps original P-51B power-required shape but worsens the P-47B and P-51B independent speed holdouts and absolute Mustang climb. We do not add separate coefficients to force a match.

Two interesting agreements and one trap: IL-2 P-51D-15 WEP and one independently reported 2020 DCS P-51D 67-inHg test each give 592 km/h at sea level, even though the test conditions and exact D variant are not matched. The IL-2 P-47D-28 gives 557 km/h at 64 inHg, very near an Eagle Dynamics developer's historical P-47D-30 table value of ~345 mph (555 km/h) at the same manifold pressure; that DCS-developer table is not a measured in-game DCS speed. A separate older DCS D-30 user run gives 615 km/h, but at 71 inHg. The 58-km/h gap is not a controlled flight-model error, because the power setting is different.

The IL-2 P-51B-5 has an actual V-1650-7 engine option matching our B-15's engine designation, and reports a 19.0-s sea-level sustained turn at 290 km/h IAS and 3,799-ft/min climb. However, its published 9,676-lb weight differs from our historical B-15 case at 9,240 lb, and its stated sea-level WEP is 1,650 hp versus our original-engine-chart 1,580 bhp node. Do not use these values to force a fictitious B-15 drag coefficient. DCS currently covers P-51D, not B-15; it covers P-47D-30 and D-40, not our original P-47B.

Original physics: NACA ACR L4I29, 1944 propeller loss charts and NACA TN 2022, actual other-prop climb loading test. Simulation specifications: IL-2 developer aircraft figures, DCS P-47D manual, DCS P-51D manual, Contact Light 2022 DCS P-51D E-M chart (self-rated low confidence), 2020 actual DCS player measurements at three heights and DCS developer's historical P-47D table. All simulation values are sanity checks, not wartime flight-test constraints. The source registry in this handover records all variant and rating warnings.

v1.7 / F-4 sustained turns & P-51B low-speed power — examined together

One engine, one aerodynamic solver, two linked gaps. The F-4's current sustained-turn spread is driven by assumed induced drag and low-speed available propulsive power. The P-51B has a documented ~115 propulsive-horsepower deficit at low-speed climb. We investigated them jointly rather than prematurely declaring either aircraft solved.

A source-backed warning about our common propeller heuristic

NACA TN 2022 (1950) directly measured three-bladed propellers on other radial fighters. In low-speed climb, higher blade loading reduced efficiency through induced loss; at high speed the opposite trend was observed from profile losses. At the current P-51B and F-4 climb operating points, our candidate-C heuristic instead predicts a small increase in η as shaft power increases 10%. This is a qualitative physics-shape warning, not authority to transfer the NACA report's numeric coefficients to four-bladed Mustangs or Bf 109 propellers. A type-relevant measured performance map remains necessary. The Mustang original Fig. 5 still overpredicts required shaft power by ~119 bhp near 318–387 mph; no hidden model tuning is applied.

Sources: IL-2 F-4 technical specifications (in-game; simulation); original NACA TN 2022 propeller test; original 20 May 1944 Wright Field P-51B Figure 5 and climb sources below. The generic model and historic P-47/P-51 top-speed holdouts remain unchanged.

v1.6 / A new test of the model where top speed cannot hide drag errors

New independent speed-regime check, no additional drag/prop coefficients fitted. The original 20 May 1944 P-51B-15 report includes a power-required curve at 22,400 ft. It tests points at 270–430 mph, beyond our single top-speed drag anchor. Most importantly, test RPM ranges from 2,100 to 3,000; v1.6 explicitly uses each recorded RPM and the real 44:21 engine/propeller reduction rather than silently assuming 3,000 throughout.

04 / Bombs, racks and external drag — a new independent challenge

Keep the same underlying three-aircraft engine, but add store weight and external parasite drag area separately. The airspeed and engine-data gates remain unchanged. The values below are hypothetical sensitivity inputs, not a historical loadout approval.

Period test — Mosquito B Mk IX LR495, same specimen, 1943 vs 1944

Estimate the fractional additional parasite drag from the lower-altitude observation, hold the assumed physical method fixed, and check it against the higher-altitude observation. Both comparisons are at different peak altitudes; true paired-condition accuracy is not proven. The RAF estimated a 15–18 mph effect after warning of deterioration between flights.

05 / New independent stores challenge — Fw 190 A-4, W.Nr. 619

Same aircraft, same sea-level combat-power reporting: the 1942 Focke-Wulf test separately records modified wheel doors, racks without bombs and four 50 kg bombs. This is a more controlled configuration sequence than the 1943/44 Mosquito reports.

Historical speed stages and an intentionally unfitted cross-aircraft transfer

The final column transfers the Mosquito's single fitted percentage only to the complete Fw 190 bomb load, not to unrelated racks or the clean aircraft; this is a deliberate stress test, not a trusted forecast. Equivalent drag increases are inferred from speed, not measured airframe coefficients. Unknown stage weight stays missing.

Further controlled configurations in a later report on W.Nr. 619

These are differences versus the clean reference within Report 3, not extra penalties to add to Report 1. Later engine/installation state is not asserted identical, and the speed values are original author's rounded differences.

New airspeed warning: a subsequent test of the same Fw 190 found that external tanks increased IAS under-reading by 6–7 km/h, through altered pitot/static pressure. If speed has already been corrected by the original report, this correction must NOT be applied again.

Sources: Focke-Wulf flight report 619/1 (4 Nov 1942) · 619/3 (20 Jan 1943), further racks/tanks comparison · 619/5 (Feb 1943), IAS-position correction. Primary manufacturer reports accessible as later online translations; image scans not independently reconciled.

04 / Cross-aircraft check — one solver, two source-reported Mustang weights

This is the deciding test, not a new fitted aircraft model. At 15,000 ft, the P-47B's open-flap climb test supplies the one fitting observation for a configuration-loss term. Four other P-47B altitudes are withheld. The P-51B receives no imported P-47 loss term; its own reported automatic cooling shutters are retained. Its level-speed-calibrated polar is frozen.

See every report observation, source weight, predicted climb and residual

Source-weight split: the 20 May 1944 Wright Field memo reports 9,335 lb at takeoff; a separate 15 May comparison memo lists 9,680 lb for climb. Both concern P-51B-15 43-24777 and are not independent aircraft/test programmes. The model uses each source's stated takeoff weight as its scenario mass, without claiming that this equals exact airborne mass.

Missing evidence: Figure 6 is ROC versus altitude; Figure 7 is power versus altitude for climb. Neither identified description provides a measured climb-speed schedule. The predicted optimum TAS in the table is therefore a model prediction, never a measured speed. A 75-inHg / 15,700-ft memo point remains unavailable because the source-bounded high-blower map does not cover that height.

Result: Candidate B better matches the Mustang's absolute climb; candidate C is better on the P-47's withheld climb tests and the Mustang's rating-induced improvement. The evidence therefore does not yet justify a single winner. No numerical coefficient was changed to make either aircraft fit.

05 / P-51B: predict the climb improvement without tuning

Wright Field Eng-47-1749-A gives 3,820 ft/min at 67 inHg and 4,380 ft/min at 75 inHg, both at 2,200 ft. We hold the aircraft's existing speed-calibrated drag polar and all propeller assumptions unchanged. The common solver computes best climb at each rating using the source-reported 9,335 lb takeoff weight as a scenario; speed-calibrated drag remains frozen. The instantaneous airborne mass is unknown.

The historical report does not give climbing airspeed in its text. Model speeds are optimization outputs, not measured flight speeds. Consequently the absolute-rate check is provisional. No P-47B fitted cooling-loss coefficient was transferred to the Mustang. No model uses these climb observations to recalibrate drag or propeller efficiency.

The report also states a +580 ft/min increase at 15,700 ft in high blower. Our 75-inHg high-blower power dataset does not cover that altitude. That second comparison remains unavailable until the relevant engine chart is transcribed; we do not extrapolate.

06 / P-47B: stop using high-speed horsepower for climbing

Wright Field reported different engine manifold pressures and cooling settings in level-speed and climb tests of the same P-47B. We now correct shaft power using the observed climb manifold pressure (approximate MAP-to-power scaling), then fit one aggregate climb-configuration loss at 15,000 ft. Every other altitude is held out from that correction.

The equivalent added drag coefficient is not a measured cooling-drag coefficient. It can include open-flap cooling drag, low-speed propeller inefficiency, uncorrected power or test-method differences. Its validity across different aircraft or other engine settings is unproven. No drag coefficient was refitted to the four withheld climb points.

07 / One Thunderbolt polar, two power settings

Same wing, 13,065-lb weight, Greg's parasite/induced drag split and his speed-dependent propulsive efficiency. Change only shaft horsepower from 2,000 to 2,600. This is a controlled sensitivity experiment using Greg's D-28-style worksheet, not a historical P-47B versus P-47D-28 flight test.

08 / Reproduce Greg's worksheet

We independently rebuild the screenshot's drag vs speed and power required from the maximum-speed row. The screenshots are treated as Greg's calculated reference, not historical test evidence.

1. Max-speed boundary

At 325 mph the 109's screenshot reports 1,218 lbf total drag and 1,058 hp propulsive power.

2. Separate components

Scale parasite drag as V² and induced drag as 1/V². Greg's supplied split is 1,137 / 81 lbf.

3. Require lift and power

Calculate required HP from drag × TAS. Then cap sustained G by provisional lift and structural limits.

09 / Compare against period flight reports

Where the report supplies an engine curve, the model predicts maximum level TAS without reading the reported speed at that altitude. The single calibration point per aircraft is identified: it is not a validation point. The F-4 additionally shows an unfitted emergency-rating check, which comes from the same published Rechlin-based synthesis as its combat anchor.

P-47B and P-51B flight-test tables are HTML transcriptions of wartime reports, not original page-by-page scan audits. P-51B power is Packard chart-derived. Sources are linked under each aircraft's details.

10 / What is known versus assumed?

Scientific limitations and next validation work

Critical: The model fits CD₀ using one reported maximum-speed anchor for each aircraft. This exactly constrains one equation but cannot independently determine both propulsive efficiency and parasite drag. The assumed Oswald parameter determines induced drag and sustained turns. The maximum-lift coefficients are provisional and therefore the stall boundary and turn curves are illustrative.

Bf 109: secondary approximate engine horsepower at 0–15,748 ft only; its sea-level 325 mph is not a matched primary test specimen, and Greg's screenshot does not provide a validated individual power-versus-altitude curve. Above this range no calculated comparison is offered.

P-47: Greg's high-power P-47 spreadsheet and Greg's high-altitude P-47B graph are separate datasets. Do not transfer 2,210 propulsive hp to the P-47B. The P-47B sourced speed tests are with cooling flaps flush, while climb testing opens shutters; no configuration-specific cooling drag yet.

Stall / airspeed: P-47 manual 115 mph IAS and P-51B flight-test 86 mph IAS are not calibrated EAS. We do not reverse-engineer exact CLmax from uncorrected IAS. CAS and TAS conversions are subsonic ISA theoretical; true IAS needs equipment/position calibration.

Propeller: Candidate A/B/C models are exploratory. Candidate C has not reproduced the six-propeller controlled P-47B experiment; no claim of NACA-validated blade efficiency is made.

Next: Validate independent climb and power-required at exact test speeds and cooling positions; seek historical low-speed CAS calibration and CLmax; test Greg's table sensitivity versus geometric e; constrain propeller class maps with P-47 propeller-swap tests; add Bf 109 source-specific test curves for higher altitudes; preserve uncertainty ranges before making ranked aircraft claims.
